meta: Agostino Carracci's engraved portrait of Titian, with a Latin dedication to Cardinal Enrico Caetani and the date 1587 at lower right.
about: Titian appears as an elderly bearded man in a skullcap and a fur-trimmed coat, seen in three-quarter view and looking off to one side. Below him runs a Latin dedication to Cardinal Enrico Caetani, who is named there as legate at Bologna. In it Agostino Carracci offers the image as a small gift and calls himself the cardinal's humble servant. He adds that the world cannot contain Titian. The date 1587 is inscribed at the lower right.

meta: Charles Willson Peale's portrait of Anne Catharine Hoof Green, the Annapolis printer who commissioned it after her husband's death.
about: Anne Catharine Hoof Green sits with one arm on a round table and a folded paper in her other hand. She was born in the Netherlands and ran a printing shop in Annapolis after her husband Jonas died in 1767. She paid his debts. She bought the building that housed the press. She then became the Maryland Assembly's official printer and published the Maryland Gazette. The museum says she commissioned this portrait two years after his death. Charles Willson Peale painted it, and he broke with one convention of female portraiture that he had learned in London.

meta: Lawrence Alma-Tadema's 1856 genre scene of a young woman giving coins to a beggar at a cottage window, painted when he was 20.
about: Sunlight falls on a cottage covered in vines. A young woman in Dutch country dress leans from an open window. She drops coins into the hat of a young man in a patched, dirty tunic. He is asking for charity on behalf of an elderly woman, who waits beside him in a wheeled, hand-drawn cart. Brick wall on the right. Distant landscape beyond. The Walters Art Museum points out that Lawrence Alma-Tadema was only 20 when he painted it. He already shows there the narrative skill that later served his scenes of Greek and Roman life.

meta: Perugino's The Baptism of Christ, a small panel from an altarpiece predella, now in the Art Institute of Chicago.
about: Christ stands in a river while Saint John the Baptist pours water over his head, and angels kneel on the banks. This small panel never hung alone. It belongs to a set of five, four now in Chicago and one showing the Resurrection in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, that formed a predella, the row of narrative scenes along the base of an altarpiece. The scenes show moments when Jesus's divine nature was revealed. The main painting above them has not been identified. Durand-Ruel bought four of the panels at a London sale in 1892 for Martin Ryerson, who left them to the Art Institute in 1933.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

meta: John William Waterhouse's Vain Lamorna, a study for his painting Lamia, showing a young woman with her hands in her hair among trees.
about: With both hands in her dark hair, a young woman tilts her head down and lowers her eyes. She wears a loose blue dress with a pale yellow neckline and stands among trees and green undergrowth beside a white bench. The picture is a study for Waterhouse's Lamia. It was sold at Christie's in 1926, at the artist's sale, under the title Vain Lamorna. William Henry Henderson of London bought it and kept it until his death in 1931. Christie's sold it twice more after that, and it is now in a private collection.

meta: Robert Henri's 1908 portrait of George Cotton Smith of Wilkes-Barre, commissioned by the sitter's daughter and given to the National Gallery of Art.
about: Pale blue eyes look out from a bearded face painted in loose, visible brushwork against a dark grey ground. The sitter is George Cotton Smith of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, who wears a dark double-breasted coat and a white collar. His daughter Amanda commissioned the portrait. Robert Henri listed it in his ledger as her property, and his diary and letters to her from 1907 deal with the Smith commissions. The back is inscribed with the sitter's name and the town. It passed to her son and then to his widow, who gave it to the museum in 1986.
credit_line: Gift of Mrs. George Cotton Smith Adams in memory of George Cotton Smith Adams

meta: Chardin's 1738 The Kitchen Maid, a woman peeling a turnip, bought from the artist by Prince Joseph Wenzel of Liechtenstein.
about: A woman in a white cap sits on a wooden chair and peels a turnip with a knife. Around her lie more turnips, a pumpkin and a basin of water holding peeled vegetables. Chardin signed and dated the picture 1738 at the right. Prince Joseph Wenzel of Liechtenstein, the Austrian ambassador to France, acquired it from the artist, and it stayed with his descendants for generations. It was shown at the Paris Salon in 1739. The dealer Frederick Mont sold it to the Samuel H. Kress Foundation in 1951, and the Foundation gave it to the National Gallery of Art the next year.

meta: Kawanabe Kyōsai's painting of a courtesan before a folding screen, her robe hiding the Seven Gods of Good Fortune.
about: Turning her head over her shoulder, a courtesan steps forward in front of a folding screen painted with a full moon and ink clouds. The obi tied in front identifies her trade, and the Cleveland Museum of Art reads her bare foot as an erotic gesture. Kawanabe Kyōsai painted this theme many times. Here he set the monochrome ink of the landscape screen against her patterned outer robe, where he hid the Seven Gods of Good Fortune. Look for them among the flowers and jewels in the pattern.

meta: A laughing boy in a blue headband and red jacket, a variant after a lost fisherboy painting by Frans Hals.
about: Laughing, with his mouth open and his head turned slightly, a boy in a blue headband and red jacket has a green cloak draped over one shoulder. The picture is a variant after a painting by Frans Hals that is presumed lost. That original showed a laughing fisherboy and dates to the late 1620s. All that survives of it is a mezzotint by Johannes de Groot. So the composition is known through the print and through variants like this one.

meta: Barthel Beham's 1528 portrait of a man in a fur collar, identified as Ruprecht Stüpf of Munich by the arms on his ring, though doubted.
about: Two red chevrons on a ring give this portrait its sitter's name. The man wears a dark robe with a broad fur collar and a black cap, and he holds a staff in front of a green curtain. The chevrons are the arms of the Stüpf family, patricians of Munich, which is why he is called Ruprecht Stüpf. The museum adds that scholars disagree. There is little firm proof that the sitters are Ruprecht and his wife Ursula Rudolph. Barthel Beham painted it in 1528.

meta: Salomon van Ruysdael's river landscape with a ferry, and the story of its seizure, recovery and restitution after Jacques Goudstikker's flight.
about: A crowded ferry carries passengers and a white horse across calm water, while cattle wade at the left bank under large trees. A turreted castle and a church steeple stand on the far shore. Salomon van Ruysdael signed the ferry itself. The dealer Jacques Goudstikker owned the picture in Amsterdam, and he left it behind when he fled the Netherlands in May 1940. The Nazis confiscated his stock and delivered it to Hermann Göring. The Allies recovered it after the war. In 2006 it was restituted to Goudstikker's daughter-in-law, and the National Gallery of Art bought it the next year.
credit_line: Patrons' Permanent Fund and The Lee and Juliet Folger Fund.  This acquisition was made possible through the generosity of the family of Jacques Goudstikker, in his memory.
